decks.title: Theory of Demand — Part 1: Meaning, Determinants and the Law of Demand
goals: Distinguish demand from desire and classify individual, market, joint, composite and derived demand
Write the demand function and explain the effect of each determinant
State the Law of Demand with its assumptions and draw a demand curve from a schedule
Explain why the demand curve slopes downward

slides.heading: Theory of Demand
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what demand means, its **kinds**, its **determinants** and the **Law of Demand**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: meaning of demand, kinds of demand, determinants, the Law of Demand, and why the curve slopes down
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Every market you visit, from a vegetable cart to an online store, runs on two forces, demand and supply. In this chapter we study the buyer's side. We will see what economists mean by demand, the different kinds of demand, what decides how much people buy, and the most famous rule in microeconomics, the Law of Demand.

slides.heading: Demand is more than a wish
slides.body_md: In economics, **demand** is the quantity of a good that buyers are **willing and able** to buy at a **given price** during a **period of time**.

nodes.label: At a price, in a period

visual.alt: Flow from desire through ability to pay and willingness to spend, stated at a price and over a period, to demand
visual.caption: Three elements plus price and time

slides.narration: Wanting something is not enough. A student may wish for an expensive laptop, but unless she can pay for it and is willing to spend that money, there is no demand in the economic sense. Demand also needs a price and a time period: we say how many kilograms a family buys at forty rupees a kilogram in a week, not just how many it buys.

slides.heading: Kinds of demand

rows: Quantity one buyer wants at each price
One family's weekly milk purchase in Ludhiana
Total of all buyers' quantities at each price
All milk bought in the town at ₹56 a litre
Two goods wanted together for one use
One good wanted for several uses
Sugarcane for sugar, jaggery and ethanol
A good or factor wanted for what it helps make
Masons wanted because flats are wanted

visual.alt: Table of five kinds of demand: individual, market, joint, composite and derived, each with its meaning and an imagined Indian example such as a gas stove with a cylinder for joint demand

slides.narration: Economists classify demand in several ways. Individual demand is one buyer, market demand is the total for all buyers. Joint demand is for goods used together, like a stove and a gas cylinder. Composite demand is one good with many uses, like sugarcane. Derived demand arises because another product is wanted, like masons for new flats.

slides.heading: Quick check: which kind of demand?
slides.body_md: Milk is used for tea, curd, paneer and sweets. Which kind of demand is this?
slides.narration: Ask yourself: is it one good with several uses, two goods used together, or a good wanted for what it helps to make?

slides.heading: What decides demand? The demand function
slides.body_md: Dx = f(Px, Py, Y, T, E)

visual.alt: Table of the non-price determinants in the demand function: a rise in the price of a substitute increases demand, of a complement decreases it; a rise in income increases demand for a normal good and decreases it for an inferior good; favourable tastes and an expected price rise increase demand
visual.caption: Dx = f(Px, Py, Y, T, E): Px moves the buyer along the curve; every other term shifts it.

slides.narration: Many things decide how much of a good a household buys. Economists write them as a demand function: the demand for good X depends on its own price, the prices of related goods, income, tastes and expectations. A dearer substitute raises demand, a dearer complement lowers it, and higher income raises demand for normal goods but lowers it for inferior goods.

slides.heading: Related goods and income
columns:
**Substitutes** can replace each other: tea and coffee, ragi and jowar flour. A dearer one raises demand for the other.

**Complements** are used together: cars and petrol, bats and balls. A dearer one lowers demand for the other.

**Normal goods:** demand rises with income (branded shoes, fine rice).

**Inferior goods:** demand falls as income rises, because buyers move to better options (coarse broken rice for some families).

visual.alt: Small table: tea and coffee are substitutes, printer and ink are complements, fine rice is a normal good for most families

slides.narration: Two relationships between goods matter. Substitutes compete with each other, so when one becomes dearer people switch to the other. Complements go together, so when one becomes dearer people buy less of both. Income matters too. For most goods demand rises with income, but for some inferior goods it falls, because better-off families switch to better options.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: using a demand function
slides.body_md: Imagined school bags, Indore: Q = 500 − 20P + 0.5Y (P and Y in ₹ hundred).
bullets: Step 1 — Substitute P = 10 and Y = 600 to get the starting quantity.
Step 2 — Change only P: the answer moves along the curve.
Step 3 — Change only Y: the whole curve shifts.

visual.alt: Worked example table for the imagined demand function Q = 500 − 20P + 0.5Y: at P 10 and Y 600 the quantity is 600 bags; at P 12 it falls to 560, a contraction; at Y 700 it rises to 650, an increase
visual.caption: Imagined school-bag market in Indore; P and Y in ₹ hundred.

slides.narration: Let us use a demand function. Start with a price of ten and an income of six hundred: the quantity is six hundred bags. If the price rises to twelve, quantity falls to five hundred and sixty, a movement up the same curve. If instead income rises to seven hundred, quantity rises to six hundred and fifty at the old price, so the whole curve has shifted.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading the function
slides.body_md: In Dx = f(Px, Py, Y, T, E), what does T stand for?
slides.narration: Recall the five letters: own price, related prices, income, tastes and expectations.

slides.heading: The Law of Demand
slides.body_md: Other things remaining the same (**ceteris paribus**), the quantity demanded of a good **rises when its price falls** and **falls when its price rises**.

rows: A change in income would shift the curve
A new fashion would change demand at every price
Expected rises make people buy now

visual.alt: Table of the assumptions of the Law of Demand: income, tastes, prices of related goods, expectations and population are held constant, each with the reason it matters

slides.narration: Now the central rule. The Law of Demand says that, other things remaining the same, price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions. The phrase other things remaining the same is vital. Income, tastes, related prices, expectations and population must stay fixed, otherwise the curve itself would move and we could not see the effect of price alone.

slides.narration: Here is Riya's weekly demand for mangoes, an imagined schedule. At one hundred and twenty rupees a kilogram she buys one kilogram; at forty rupees she buys five. Plotting each pair, with quantity across and price up, gives a curve that slopes downward from left to right. Every point on it answers one question: at this price, how much does she buy?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: drawing Riya's demand curve
bullets: Step 1 — Quantity on the x-axis, price on the y-axis.
Step 3 — Join them: a downward-sloping straight line, Q = 7 − P/20.
Step 4 — Label it DD and name the law it shows.

visual.alt: Riya's imagined mango schedule: 1 kg at 120 rupees, 2 at 100, 3 at 80, 4 at 60 and 5 at 40

slides.narration: Examiners often give a schedule and ask for the curve. Put quantity on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical axis, plot each pair, and join them. Riya's points lie on a straight line, because every twenty-rupee fall adds one kilogram. Label the curve and say which law it illustrates. Neat labels on both axes carry marks.

slides.heading: Why does the curve slope downward?

nodes.label: Substitution effect: it is cheaper than its substitutes
Diminishing marginal utility and new buyers
More is demanded: the curve slopes downward

visual.alt: Flow showing the reasons for the downward slope: a fall in price works through the substitution effect, the income effect, diminishing marginal utility and new buyers, so more is demanded
visual.caption: Why the demand curve slopes downward

slides.narration: Why do people buy more when the price falls? First, the substitution effect: the good is now cheaper than its substitutes. Second, the income effect: the same money buys more, so real income rises. Third, diminishing marginal utility: extra units are worth less, so people buy them only at a lower price. Fourth, new buyers who could not afford it before now enter the market.

slides.heading: Quick check: which effect?
slides.body_md: Guavas become cheaper while apples cost the same, and a family buys more guavas and fewer apples. Which effect is this?
slides.narration: Is it about the relative price of two goods, or about how far the family's money now goes?

slides.heading: Income effect versus substitution effect

rows: Guavas replace some apples in the fruit basket
The same budget now buys more fruit

visual.alt: Two-row table contrasting the substitution effect, which works through the relative price, and the income effect, which works through real income, with a guava example

slides.narration: These two effects are easy to mix up. The substitution effect works through relative prices: guavas replace apples because they are cheaper by comparison. The income effect works through purchasing power: the same budget now stretches further. For normal goods both push in the same direction, which is why the demand curve slopes downward so reliably.

slides.body_md: Using Riya's schedule, by how many kilograms does her purchase rise when the price falls from ₹100 to ₹60?
slides.narration: Read the two quantities from the schedule and subtract.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Desire + ability + willingness, at a price, over a period
Dx = f(Px, Py, Y, T, E)
Substitution, income, diminishing MU, new buyers

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: meaning and kinds of demand, the demand function, the Law of Demand and the reasons for its downward slope

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Demand is desire backed by ability and willingness to pay, at a price and over a period. It can be individual, market, joint, composite or derived. Its determinants are written as a demand function. The Law of Demand states an inverse relation between price and quantity demanded, other things equal, and four reasons explain the downward slope.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Always write "other things remaining the same" when stating the law.
Put **quantity on the x-axis** and **price on the y-axis**; label the curve DD.
Classify related goods first (substitute or complement), then predict the direction.
For inferior goods a higher income **lowers** demand; do not assume all goods are normal.
2 marks: two clear points; 3 marks: three points or a point with a diagram; 5 marks: parts answered in order.
slides.narration: A few habits earn marks in this chapter. Always state the law with the phrase other things remaining the same. Put quantity on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical axis, and label every curve. Decide whether goods are substitutes or complements before predicting a change. And remember that inferior goods behave differently when income rises.

slides.heading: Theory of Demand — Part 2
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **market demand**, **movements versus shifts**, and **exceptions** to the law.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: market demand, movement along the curve, shift of the curve, and exceptions to the law
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In Part 2 we build the market demand curve from individual buyers, learn the most tested distinction in this chapter, between moving along a demand curve and shifting it, and finally meet the cases where people buy more of a good at a higher price.

slides.heading: Market demand: add quantities at each price
slides.body_md: Market demand at a price = **sum of the quantities** all buyers want at that price (**horizontal summation**).

visual.alt: Worked example: three students' daily samosa demand and the market total at each price: 15 at 10 rupees, 11 at 15 rupees, 8 at 20 rupees, 4 at 25 rupees
visual.caption: Imagined Nagpur college canteen. Market = sum across each row.

slides.narration: A market is many buyers. To get market demand, take one price at a time, read what each buyer wants at that price, and add the quantities. In this imagined canteen, at ten rupees Asha wants five samosas, Bilal four and Charu six, so the market wants fifteen. Repeating this at every price gives the market schedule.

slides.narration: Graphically, we add the individual curves sideways, which is why it is called horizontal summation. In this imagined Kochi example, household A stops buying at eighty rupees, so above that price the market curve is the same as household B's. Below eighty both households buy, the market curve becomes flatter, and there is a kink at eighty rupees.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: building a market schedule
slides.body_md: Add across each row of the canteen schedules.

visual.alt: Market samosa schedule: 15 at 10 rupees, 11 at 15 rupees, 8 at 20 rupees, 4 at 25 rupees

slides.narration: Let us finish the canteen example. At each price, add the three students' quantities. The market schedule is fifteen samosas at ten rupees, eleven at fifteen, eight at twenty and four at twenty-five. The market curve drawn from these figures lies to the right of every individual curve and still slopes downward.

slides.heading: Quick check: how is market demand formed?
slides.body_md: True or false: market demand is found by adding the prices different buyers will pay for the same quantity.
slides.narration: Think about what you added in the canteen example: prices or quantities?

slides.heading: Movement along versus shift

visual.alt: Table contrasting a movement along the demand curve, caused by the own price and called extension or contraction on one curve, with a shift of the curve, caused by other determinants and called increase or decrease

slides.narration: This is the distinction examiners love. If only the good's own price changes, the buyer moves along the same demand curve: down for an extension, up for a contraction. If anything else changes, such as income, tastes or the price of a related good, the whole curve shifts: right for an increase, left for a decrease.

slides.heading: Giffen goods versus Veblen goods
columns: **Giffen good:** an inferior necessity taking a large share of a poor family's budget. A price rise cuts real income so sharply that the family buys **more** of it and less of costlier food.
**Veblen good:** a luxury bought partly for **status**. A higher price makes it more exclusive and so more desirable to rich buyers.

visual.alt: Comparison table of Giffen and Veblen goods: buyers, kind of good and the reason the demand curve can slope upward

slides.narration: Do not confuse the two upward-sloping cases. A Giffen good is an inferior necessity of very poor households; its strong income effect outweighs the substitution effect. A Veblen good is a luxury of rich households; its price itself signals status. Every Giffen good is inferior, but most inferior goods still obey the law.

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2. Market demand is the horizontal sum of individual demands. A change in the good's own price moves buyers along the curve, an extension or a contraction. A change in any other determinant shifts the curve, an increase or a decrease. Giffen goods, Veblen goods, expectations and emergencies are exceptions to the law.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Movement = one curve, two points; shift = two curves, one price.
Use the words **extension/contraction** for movements and **increase/decrease** for shifts.
Market demand: add **quantities**, never prices; watch for buyers who drop out above some price.
Giffen: poor households, inferior staple, income effect dominates; Veblen: rich households, status.
Numericals are set on schedules: show the addition at each price.
slides.narration: Common slips cost marks here. Do not call a price-led change an increase in demand; call it an extension. Draw one curve for a movement and two curves for a shift. When building market demand, add quantities at each price and note when a buyer drops out. And keep Giffen and Veblen goods apart: who buys, what kind of good, and why.

sections.heading: 1. Meaning and kinds of demand
sections.body_md:
**Demand** is the quantity of a good that buyers are **willing and able** to purchase at a **given price** during a **given period**. A wish without the means to pay is only a desire.

- **Individual demand:** one buyer's quantities at different prices.
- **Market demand:** the total of all buyers' quantities at each price.
- **Joint demand:** goods wanted together (stove and LPG cylinder).
- **Composite demand:** one good with several uses (electricity for lighting, cooking and pumps).
- **Derived demand:** wanted for what it helps to produce (labour for construction).

key_terms.definition_md: Desire backed by ability and willingness to pay, at a price, over a period.
Demand for a good or factor that arises from the demand for another product.

rows: Quantity one buyer wants at each price
One family's weekly milk purchase in Ludhiana
Total of all buyers' quantities at each price
All milk bought in the town at ₹56 a litre
Two goods wanted together for one use
One good wanted for several uses
Sugarcane for sugar, jaggery and ethanol
A good or factor wanted for what it helps make
Masons wanted because flats are wanted

sections.heading: 2. Determinants and the demand function
sections.body_md:
**Dx = f(Px, Py, Y, T, E)** — own price, prices of related goods, income, tastes and expectations (population matters for market demand).

- A dearer **substitute** raises demand; a dearer **complement** lowers it.
- Higher income raises demand for a **normal** good and lowers it for an **inferior** good.
- A shift of **tastes** towards the good, or an **expected** price rise, raises demand now.

The own price causes movements along the curve; every other determinant shifts it.

key_terms.definition_md: Goods that can replace each other, such as tea and coffee.
Goods used together, such as cars and petrol.
A good whose demand falls as income rises.

sections.heading: 3. The Law of Demand
sections.body_md:
**Statement:** ceteris paribus, quantity demanded varies **inversely** with price.

**Assumptions:** income, tastes, prices of related goods, expectations and population stay constant.

A **demand schedule** lists price–quantity pairs; plotting them (quantity on the x-axis, price on the y-axis) gives the **demand curve**, which slopes downward.

**Reasons for the downward slope:** substitution effect; income effect; diminishing marginal utility; new buyers entering; more uses found for a cheaper good.

key_terms.definition_md: Buying more of a good because it has become relatively cheaper.
Buying more because a lower price raises real income.

sections.heading: 4. Market demand
sections.body_md:
Market demand is found by **horizontal summation**: at each price, add the quantities of all buyers. If a buyer stops buying above some price, the market curve above that price is made of the remaining buyers only, which can create a **kink**.

The market curve lies to the right of every individual curve and slopes downward.

sections.heading: 5. Movement along and shift of the demand curve
sections.body_md:
- **Change in quantity demanded** (own price): **extension** when the price falls, **contraction** when it rises — a movement along one curve.
- **Change in demand** (other determinants): **increase** (rightward shift) or **decrease** (leftward shift) — two curves.

To classify any event, first check whether the own price changed.

sections.heading: 6. Exceptions to the Law of Demand
sections.body_md:
- **Giffen goods:** inferior necessities of the very poor; a strong negative income effect outweighs the substitution effect.
- **Veblen goods:** status goods whose appeal rises with their price.
- **Expectations:** buyers who expect further rises buy more now.
- **Emergencies:** essentials bought whatever the price.

In these cases the demand curve may slope upward over some range.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing "increase in demand" for a price-led change (it is an **extension**).
- Drawing one curve for a shift, or two curves for a movement.
- Adding prices instead of quantities when building market demand.
- Treating every good as normal: for an inferior good a higher income lowers demand.
- Confusing Giffen goods (poor households, inferior staple) with Veblen goods (rich households, status).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: the correct option or a one-line answer.
- 2 marks: two clear points, or a point with a labelled diagram.
- 3 marks: three points, or a calculation with its interpretation.
- 5 marks: each part answered in order, with labelled diagrams where asked.
- Board papers also set 4-mark (2 + 2) and 8-mark (4 + 4) questions in parts: answer each part separately.

questions.stem_md: Kabir, a Class 12 student in an imagined hill town, would love a ₹90,000 gaming laptop but has no savings and no one will pay for it. In economics, his wish for the laptop is

options.text_md: effective demand, because he is willing to buy
a desire only, because it is not backed by the ability to pay
market demand, because many students share it
derived demand, because he needs the laptop for study

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a desire only, because it is not backed by the ability to pay. Demand needs desire, ability to pay and willingness to spend, at a given price and time. Kabir lacks the means, so it is only a desire. Market demand is a total over buyers, and derived demand arises from the demand for another product.

questions.stem_md: Hostel residents in an imagined Pune college buy bread and butter together for breakfast; neither is bought alone. The demand for these two goods is an example of

options.text_md: composite demand
derived demand
competitive demand
joint demand

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** joint demand. Goods demanded together to satisfy one want have joint demand. Composite demand is one good wanted for several uses; derived demand comes from the demand for another product; competitive demand describes substitutes.

questions.stem_md: A dairy in an imagined Anand-like town sells milk that households use for tea, curd, paneer and sweets. The demand for milk in this situation is

options.text_md: composite demand
joint demand
derived demand
individual demand

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** composite demand. When one good is demanded for several different uses, its demand is composite. Joint demand is two goods used together; derived demand flows from demand for another good.

questions.stem_md: A new township is being built near an imagined Raipur suburb, and builders are hiring many more masons and plumbers. The demand for these workers is called

options.text_md: composite demand
joint demand
derived demand
autonomous demand

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** derived demand. Labour is wanted because houses are wanted: its demand is derived from the demand for the final product. The other terms describe different relationships between goods.

questions.stem_md: The market demand for a commodity at a given price refers to

options.text_md: the quantity that the richest buyer will buy at that price
the average quantity bought by one household over a year
the sum of the quantities that all buyers in the market will buy at that price
the quantity that sellers wish to sell at that price

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the sum of the quantities that all buyers in the market will buy at that price. Market demand adds up individual quantities demanded at each price. One buyer's quantity is individual demand, and what sellers wish to sell is supply.

questions.stem_md: Builders want cement only because households want new flats. The demand for cement is therefore called ___ demand.
questions.solution_md: Cement is wanted for the final product it helps to make, so its demand is derived demand.

questions.stem_md: Match each imagined situation from a town in Odisha with the kind of demand it shows.

options.text_md: Ink cartridges and printers bought together by an office
Electricity used for lighting, cooking and pumping water
A bakery hiring more bakers as cake orders rise
The total quantity of rice bought by all families in the town at a price

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Goods used together have joint demand; one good with many uses has composite demand; a factor wanted for what it helps produce has derived demand; the total over all buyers at a price is market demand.

questions.stem_md: How does demand in economics differ from a mere desire? Illustrate with a student who wants a scooter.
questions.solution_md: Three elements of demand plus the price and time qualification, with the scooter example.

answer.model_answer_md: A **desire** is only a wish. **Demand** is a desire backed by the **ability to pay** and the **willingness to spend**, stated at a **given price** for a **period of time**. A student who wants a scooter but cannot pay for it has only a desire.

marking_scheme.step: Elements of demand: desire, ability, willingness
Price and time reference with the example

questions.stem_md: Distinguish joint demand from composite demand, giving one Indian example of each.
questions.solution_md: Contrast "several goods, one use" with "one good, several uses", each with an example.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Joint demand:** two or more goods are wanted **together** for one purpose, such as a gas stove and an LPG cylinder.
**Composite demand:** **one good** is wanted for **several uses**, such as sugarcane used for sugar, jaggery and ethanol.

questions.stem_md: Identify the kind of demand in each imagined case from a Mysuru market and give a reason: (i) a silk-weaving unit employs more weavers as saree orders grow; (ii) a family buys a mobile phone and a SIM card together; (iii) coal is bought by a power plant, a brick kiln and a hotel kitchen.
questions.solution_md: One mark for each correct kind with its reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Derived demand:** the unit hires weavers only because buyers want sarees; the demand for labour comes from the demand for the final product.
(ii) **Joint demand:** the phone is useless without a SIM card and the card without a phone, so the two are demanded together to meet one want.
(iii) **Composite demand:** a single good, coal, is wanted by three different users for three different purposes.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined Chennai neighbourhood the price of filter coffee powder rises sharply while the price of tea leaves stays the same. Other things equal, the demand curve for tea leaves will

options.text_md: shift to the right, because tea and coffee are substitutes
shift to the left, because tea and coffee are complements
not move, because the price of tea is unchanged
show a contraction along the same curve

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** shift to the right, because tea and coffee are substitutes. Coffee and tea are substitutes, so a dearer coffee makes buyers switch to tea: more tea is demanded at every price and the curve shifts right. A contraction would need a rise in the price of tea itself.

questions.stem_md: If the price of petrol in an imagined district rises steeply, the demand for petrol motorcycles there is most likely to

options.text_md: increase, because petrol and motorcycles are substitutes
extend, because motorcycles become cheaper
remain unchanged, because the price of motorcycles has not changed
decrease, because petrol and motorcycles are complements

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** decrease, because petrol and motorcycles are complements. Motorcycles and petrol are used together (complements). Dearer petrol raises the cost of riding, so fewer motorcycles are demanded at each price: a decrease, a leftward shift.

questions.stem_md: When the incomes of families in an imagined Bihar village rise, they buy less coarse broken rice and more fine rice. For these families, coarse broken rice is

options.text_md: a normal good
an inferior good
a Veblen good
a complementary good

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** an inferior good. A good whose demand falls as income rises has a negative income effect: it is an inferior good. Fine rice, whose demand rises, is a normal good.

questions.stem_md: In the demand function Dx = f(Px, Py, Y, T, E), the letter T stands for

options.text_md: the tastes and preferences of the consumer
the tax rate on the good
the time period of supply
the technology used by producers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the tastes and preferences of the consumer. T is tastes and preferences. Px is the own price, Py prices of related goods, Y income and E expectations; tax and technology are determinants of supply, not demand.

questions.stem_md: Shoppers in an imagined Surat market hear that the price of cooking oil will rise sharply next week. The most likely effect this week is

options.text_md: a contraction in the quantity of cooking oil demanded
an increase in the demand for cooking oil at the present price
a decrease in the demand for cooking oil
no change, because the present price has not changed

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** an increase in the demand for cooking oil at the present price. Expected future price is a determinant of demand. Buyers stock up now, so demand at today's price rises (a rightward shift). Contraction and decrease would need a price rise now or a fall in demand.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A rise in household income shifts the demand curve for a normal good to the right.

**Reason (R):** A normal good has a positive income effect: more is bought at each price when income rises.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and the positive income effect is exactly why more is demanded at every price, so R explains A.

questions.stem_md: True or false? If printers become much cheaper, the demand for printer ink cartridges falls, because the two goods are complements.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** For complements a fall in the price of one good raises the demand for the other: cheaper printers mean more printers in use and more cartridges demanded, so the statement is false.

questions.stem_md: The monthly demand for an imagined brand of school bags in Indore is Q = 500 − 20P + 0.5Y, where P is price and Y is average family income (both in ₹ hundred). Find Q when P = 10 and Y = 600.
Explain how a rise in the price of a related good affects the demand for a good when the two are substitutes and when they are complements.
questions.solution_md: Direction of change for each relationship, with an example.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Substitutes** (such as tea and coffee): when coffee becomes dearer, buyers switch to tea, so the **demand for tea increases**.
**Complements** (such as cars and petrol): when petrol becomes dearer, **fewer cars are demanded**, so demand decreases.

questions.stem_md: A family in an imagined Jaipur colony gets a pay rise and buys fewer bus tickets but more autorickshaw rides. Classify both services and justify your answer.
questions.solution_md: Classification from the direction of the income effect for each service.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Bus tickets** are an **inferior good** for this family: demand falls as income rises (negative income effect).
**Autorickshaw rides** are a **normal good**: demand rises with income (positive income effect).

questions.stem_md: Other than the price of the good itself, explain any three factors that decide how much of a good a household demands.
questions.solution_md: Any three non-price determinants, each with the direction of its effect.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Income:** for a normal good a higher income raises demand; for an inferior good it lowers demand.
2. **Prices of related goods:** a dearer substitute raises demand; a dearer complement lowers it.
3. **Tastes and preferences:** a good that becomes fashionable, or is advertised well, is demanded more at each price. (Also: expectations of future prices, population.)

questions.stem_md: For the imagined school-bag demand Q = 500 − 20P + 0.5Y (P and Y in ₹ hundred), with P = 10 and Y = 600 at first, find the quantity demanded after (i) the price rises to 12 with income unchanged, and (ii) income rises to 700 with the price at 10. State whether each is a movement along or a shift of the demand curve.
questions.solution_md: Substitute each change into the function and classify by whether the own price or another determinant changed.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Q = 500 − 20 × 12 + 0.5 × 600 = **560** bags: own price changed, so a **movement along** the curve (contraction from 600).
(ii) Q = 500 − 20 × 10 + 0.5 × 700 = **650** bags: income changed, so the curve **shifts** to the right (an increase in demand).

questions.stem_md: Before an announced rise in gold prices, jewellery shops in an imagined Thrissur market are crowded even though prices have already gone up a little. Explain how expectations can make buyers demand more at a higher price, and say whether this breaks the law of demand.
questions.solution_md: Expectation effect, the resulting shift, and the link to the ceteris paribus assumption.

answer.model_answer_md: Buyers **expect the price to rise further**, so buying now looks cheaper than buying later. Demand at every present price **increases**, so they buy more even though the price is higher. The law of demand assumes **expectations stay constant**; since that assumption is broken, this is an **exception**, not a contradiction of the law.

marking_scheme.step: More bought at a higher price
Exception because the assumption is broken

questions.stem_md: Write the demand function for a good X and explain how each of its determinants affects the demand for X. (a) Write the function and name its terms. [2] (b) Explain the effect of any three determinants other than the own price. [3]
questions.solution_md: Function with named terms, then three determinants with directions.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Dx = f(Px, Py, Y, T, E)**: Dx is the demand for X; **Px** its own price; **Py** prices of related goods; **Y** the consumer's income; **T** tastes and preferences; **E** expectations of future prices.
(b) 1. **Py:** a dearer **substitute** raises Dx; a dearer **complement** lowers Dx.
2. **Y:** for a **normal** good a higher income raises Dx; for an **inferior** good it lowers Dx.
3. **T:** a shift of taste towards X (fashion, health awareness, advertising) raises Dx at every price.
A change in Px moves the buyer **along** the curve; a change in any other determinant **shifts** it.

questions.stem_md: Other things remaining the same, the Law of Demand states that the quantity demanded of a good

options.text_md: rises when its price rises
stays the same whatever its price
falls when its price rises and rises when its price falls
depends only on the income of the consumer

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** falls when its price rises and rises when its price falls. The law states an inverse relation between own price and quantity demanded, with all other determinants held constant.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is NOT an assumption of the Law of Demand?

options.text_md: Tastes and preferences remain unchanged
Prices of related goods remain constant
No change is expected in the future price
The consumer's income rises as the price falls

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The consumer's income rises as the price falls. The law holds income constant. If income changed along with price, the demand curve itself would shift and the law could not be isolated.

questions.stem_md: When guavas become cheaper while apples cost the same, a family in an imagined Allahabad colony buys more guavas and fewer apples. This reason for the downward slope of the demand curve for guavas is the

options.text_md: income effect
Veblen effect
bandwagon effect
substitution effect

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** substitution effect. Guavas are now relatively cheaper than apples, so the family substitutes guavas for apples. The income effect works through a rise in real income instead.

Riya's weekly demand for mangoes in an imagined Lucknow colony is given below. How many kilograms does she buy when the price is ₹80 per kg?

| 120 | 1 |

4 kg
3 kg

questions.stem_md: Using Riya's mango schedule (Q = 7 − P/20, imagined), by how many kilograms does her weekly purchase rise when the price falls from ₹100 to ₹60 per kg?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: At ₹100, Q = 7 − 5 = 2 kg; at ₹60, Q = 7 − 3 = 4 kg.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A consumer buys more units of a good only when its price falls.

**Reason (R):** Each additional unit gives less marginal utility, so the consumer pays less for it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. Because marginal utility diminishes, the consumer will buy an extra unit only at a lower price, which explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When the price of air-coolers falls, some families who could not afford one earlier start buying it.

**Reason (R):** Market demand is obtained by adding the quantities demanded by all buyers at each price.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but R only defines market demand. It does not explain why new buyers enter at a lower price (that is the fall in price relative to their means), so R is not the explanation of A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Law of Demand assumes that the tastes of the consumer do not change.

**Reason (R):** The Law of Demand holds even when the consumer's income changes at the same time as the price.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false: the law needs income to be constant; if income changes with price, the curve shifts and the inverse relation cannot be isolated.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Law of Demand shows a direct relationship between the price of a good and the quantity demanded.

**Reason (R):** For normal goods the demand curve slopes upward from left to right.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are false. The law describes an inverse relationship, and for normal goods the demand curve slopes downward.

questions.stem_md: The Law of Demand holds under the condition of ___, that is, other things remaining the same.
questions.solution_md: The phrase is ceteris paribus: all determinants other than the own price stay constant.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps for drawing Riya's demand curve for mangoes from her schedule in the correct order.

options.text_md: Join the points to get a curve sloping down from left to right
Draw the axes: quantity on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical axis
Plot one point for each price–quantity pair in the schedule
Choose a scale for each axis to fit the schedule

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (d) → (c) → (a). Axes first, then scales, then the plotted pairs, and finally the joined curve.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Give any two reasons why the demand curve for an ordinary good slopes downward.
questions.solution_md: Any two valid reasons, each explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Substitution effect:** a cheaper good replaces now-dearer substitutes, so more of it is bought.
2. **Income effect:** a lower price raises the buyer's real income, so more of a normal good is bought. (Also: diminishing marginal utility; new buyers enter; more uses become worthwhile.)

From Riya's imagined weekly mango schedule below, describe the demand curve you would draw, state the law it illustrates, and name one assumption behind it.

| 120 | 1 |
| 100 | 2 |
| 80 | 3 |
| 60 | 4 |

questions.solution_md: Correct plotting description, the law, and one ceteris paribus assumption.

answer.model_answer_md: Plot quantity (kg) on the x-axis and price on the y-axis; the points (1, 120), (2, 100), (3, 80), (4, 60) and (5, 40) lie on a **straight line sloping downward**. questions.stem_md: The price of a popular brand of instant noodles falls by a third in an imagined Shillong market. Using the income effect and the substitution effect, explain why students there buy more packets.
questions.solution_md: Explain each effect in the context and combine them.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Substitution effect:** the noodles become cheaper **relative to** snacks like biscuits and momos, so students switch towards noodles.
**Income effect:** with the same pocket money they can now buy more packets, as their **real income** has risen.
Both effects point the same way for a normal good, so the **quantity demanded rises** and the demand curve slopes downward.

questions.stem_md: Explain the Law of Demand for a good sold in an imagined Kanpur market. (a) State the law and any two of its assumptions. [2] (b) Construct an imagined demand schedule of four rows and describe the demand curve drawn from it. [3]
questions.solution_md: Statement and assumptions, then a consistent inverse schedule and its curve.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Law:** other things remaining the same, the quantity demanded of a good **rises when its price falls** and **falls when its price rises**. Assumptions: the consumer's **income** and **tastes** do not change (also: prices of related goods and expectations are constant).
(b) Imagined weekly demand for guavas by one family:

| Price (₹ per kg) | Quantity (kg) |
|---|---|
| 80 | 1 |
| 60 | 2 |
| 40 | 3 |
| 20 | 4 |

With price on the y-axis and quantity on the x-axis, the points form a curve **sloping downward from left to right**: each fall in price is matched by a rise in the quantity bought.

questions.stem_md: Why does the demand curve of an ordinary good slope downward from left to right? Explain any five reasons with examples from an Indian household.
questions.solution_md: Five distinct reasons, each linked to a household example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Diminishing marginal utility:** each extra kilogram of sugar gives less satisfaction, so a family buys more only at a lower price.
2. **Substitution effect:** when tea becomes cheaper relative to coffee, the family substitutes tea for coffee.
3. **Income effect:** a fall in the price of pulses frees part of the budget, so **real income** rises and more pulses are bought.
4. **New buyers:** a lower price brings families who could not afford the good earlier into the market.
5. **Several uses:** a cheaper good such as milk is put to more uses (sweets, curd) besides tea.
Together these make quantity demanded rise as price falls.

questions.stem_md: The market demand curve is obtained from individual demand curves by

options.text_md: adding the prices that each buyer would pay for a given quantity (vertical summation)
adding the quantities demanded by all buyers at each price (horizontal summation)
taking the average of the individual curves
choosing the demand curve of the largest buyer

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** adding the quantities demanded by all buyers at each price (horizontal summation). At each price we add the quantities: a horizontal summation. Adding prices would be a vertical summation, which is not how market demand is formed.

True or false? The market demand curve is found by adding the prices that different buyers are willing to pay for the same quantity.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Market demand adds quantities at each price (horizontal summation); adding prices for a given quantity is a vertical summation and does not give market demand.

questions.stem_md: Explain in two steps how a market demand schedule is built from the schedules of individual buyers.
questions.solution_md: Price-by-price reading, then horizontal addition.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Take **each price** in turn and note the quantity that **every buyer** wants at that price.
2. **Add these quantities** to get the market quantity at that price; listing these totals against the prices gives the market demand schedule.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined Kochi households buy banana chips: A demands Q = 8 − 0.1P and B demands Q = 6 − 0.05P (P in ₹ per packet; quantities cannot be negative). (a) Prepare the market demand schedule at ₹40, ₹60, ₹80 and ₹100. [3] (b) Describe how the market demand curve is derived and why it has a kink. [2]
questions.solution_md: Correct schedule, then horizontal summation and the reason for the kink at ₹80.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a)

| Price (₹) | A | B | Market |
|---|---|---|---|
| 40 | 4 | 4 | 8 |
| 60 | 2 | 3 | 5 |
| 80 | 0 | 2 | 2 |
| 100 | 0 | 1 | 1 |

(b) The market curve is the **horizontal sum** of A's and B's curves: at each price their quantities are added. Above ₹80 only B buys (A's quantity is zero), so the market curve **coincides with B's curve**; below ₹80 both buy, so the market curve becomes **flatter**. This change at ₹80 gives the curve a **kink**.

Quantities of B at all prices

questions.stem_md: A fall in the price of onions, with nothing else changing, leads buyers in an imagined Nashik market to buy more onions. This is called

options.text_md: an increase in demand (a rightward shift)
an extension of demand (a downward movement along the curve)
a contraction of demand
a decrease in demand

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** an extension of demand (a downward movement along the curve). Only the own price changed, so buyers move down along the same curve: an extension. A shift would need a change in another determinant.

questions.stem_md: Teachers in an imagined Dehradun school receive a large salary arrear. For a normal good such as branded shoes, the effect is shown by

options.text_md: a movement up along the demand curve
a leftward shift of the demand curve
a movement down along the demand curve
a rightward shift of the demand curve

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a rightward shift of the demand curve. Higher income raises the demand for a normal good at every price: an increase in demand, shown by a rightward shift.

questions.stem_md: The price of cricket balls rises sharply in an imagined Meerut sports market. What happens to the demand curve for cricket bats?

options.text_md: It shifts to the left (a decrease in demand)
It shifts to the right (an increase in demand)
There is a contraction along the curve
There is an extension along the curve

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It shifts to the left (a decrease in demand). Bats and balls are complements; dearer balls mean fewer bats are demanded at every bat price, so the bat demand curve shifts left. A contraction would need a rise in the price of bats.

questions.stem_md: On a demand curve DD for kites in an imagined Ahmedabad market, point B shows 40 kites at ₹15 and point A shows 25 kites at ₹20. Moving from B to A shows

options.text_md: an increase in demand caused by a rise in income
an extension of demand caused by a fall in price
a contraction of demand caused by a rise in price
a decrease in demand caused by a change in tastes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a contraction of demand caused by a rise in price. Both points are on the same curve and the price rose from ₹15 to ₹20 while quantity fell: a contraction (upward movement along the curve).

questions.stem_md: A demand curve for green tea in an imagined Guwahati market shifts from D₁ to D₂, so that at an unchanged price of ₹200 a packet buyers now want 30 packets instead of 20. Which event could have caused this?

options.text_md: A fall in the price of green tea
A fall in the price of a close substitute, ordinary tea
A health campaign that makes green tea fashionable
A rise in the price of green tea

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A health campaign that makes green tea fashionable. More is demanded at the same price, so the curve shifted right. A favourable change in tastes does this. Changes in the own price only move buyers along a curve, and a cheaper substitute would shift it left.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An increase in demand is shown by a rightward shift of the demand curve.

**Reason (R):** A rise in the price of the good itself raises the quantity demanded of it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false: a rise in the own price lowers the quantity demanded (a contraction), and in any case an own-price change never shifts the curve.

questions.stem_md: A change in demand caused by a factor other than the good's own price is shown by a ___ of the demand curve.
questions.solution_md: Non-price factors move the whole curve: a shift (right for an increase, left for a decrease).

questions.stem_md: Match each imagined event in a Bengaluru market for fresh juice with the change it causes.

options.text_md: The juice shop cuts its own price
The juice shop raises its own price
A heatwave makes cold drinks more desirable
A cheaper soft drink is launched next door

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Own-price changes cause extension or contraction along the curve; a favourable change in tastes increases demand; a cheaper substitute decreases it.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between a change in quantity demanded and a change in demand.
questions.solution_md: Cause and graphical representation of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Change in quantity demanded:** caused only by a change in the good's **own price**; shown by a **movement along** the same curve (extension or contraction).
**Change in demand:** caused by **other determinants** such as income or tastes; shown by a **shift** of the curve (increase or decrease).

marking_scheme.step: Change in quantity demanded: cause and movement
Change in demand: cause and shift

questions.stem_md: A juice seller in an imagined Madurai street sells more glasses one week. Explain how you would decide whether this reflects an extension of demand or an increase in demand.
questions.solution_md: The test is whether the own price or another determinant changed.

answer.model_answer_md: Check **what changed**. If the seller **cut the price** and nothing else changed, buyers moved down the same curve: an **extension**. If the price stayed the same but, say, the weather turned hotter or incomes rose, the whole curve shifted right: an **increase**.

questions.stem_md: Predict the effect on the demand curve for petrol scooters in an imagined Ranchi market in each case: (i) the price of scooters falls; (ii) petrol becomes much dearer; (iii) a bank offers cheap scooter loans that raise buyers' purchasing power.
questions.solution_md: One mark per case: correct change with its reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Extension:** a movement down along the same curve, since only the own price fell.
(ii) **Decrease:** a **leftward shift**, because petrol is a complement and riding becomes costlier.
(iii) **Increase:** a **rightward shift**, since buyers can afford more scooters at every price.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish a contraction of demand from a decrease in demand, with one imagined example of each from a Kolkata sweet shop and a description of the diagram for each.
questions.solution_md: Cause, example and diagram for each, with a clear contrast.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Contraction:** the shop **raises the price** of rasgullas and buyers move **up along the same curve** to a smaller quantity (point to point on one curve).
**Decrease:** at the **same price**, buyers want fewer rasgullas because, say, a health scare changes tastes; the **whole curve shifts left** (D₁ to D₂).
So the first is caused by the own price, the second by another determinant.

questions.stem_md: Using imagined data for tickets at a cinema hall in an imagined Kozhikode town, explain with diagrams (a) the difference between extension and contraction of demand [2], and (b) the difference between increase and decrease in demand, naming one cause of each [3].
questions.solution_md: Movements on one curve, then shifts with causes, linked to diagrams.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) On one demand curve DD: when the ticket price **falls from ₹200 to ₹150**, sales rise from 300 to 400 a show: an **extension** (movement **down** the curve). When the price **rises back**, sales fall: a **contraction** (movement **up** the curve). Only the own price changes.
(b) At an unchanged price of ₹200, the curve shifts **right** from D₁ to D₂ (say 300 to 380 tickets) when a much-awaited film is released: an **increase in demand** due to tastes. It shifts **left** from D₁ to D₀ when a new multiplex opens nearby (a **substitute**): a **decrease in demand**.
Movements come from own-price changes; shifts from other determinants.

marking_scheme.step: Overall contrast of movement and shift

questions.stem_md: A Giffen good is best described as an inferior good

options.text_md: for which the negative income effect of a price change outweighs the substitution effect
that is bought only to show off wealth
whose price is fixed by the government
for which the substitution effect outweighs the income effect

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** for which the negative income effect of a price change outweighs the substitution effect. For a Giffen good the strong negative income effect dominates, so a price rise increases quantity demanded. Showing off wealth describes Veblen goods.

questions.stem_md: An imagined luxury watch brand in Mumbai doubles its prices and finds that more wealthy buyers want its watches, because owning one signals status. These watches are behaving as

options.text_md: Giffen goods
inferior goods
complementary goods
Veblen (prestige) goods

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Veblen (prestige) goods. Goods bought for display of status, whose desirability rises with price, are Veblen goods. Giffen goods are inferior necessities of the poor.

questions.stem_md: After a flood warning in an imagined Assam district, families buy more candles and drinking water even though shop prices have risen. This is an exception to the Law of Demand because of

options.text_md: a Veblen effect
an emergency
a fall in income
ignorance about prices

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** an emergency. During emergencies people buy more of essentials whatever the price, so the usual inverse relation does not hold.

questions.stem_md: When the price of shares of an imagined company starts rising, more investors rush to buy them. Which exception to the Law of Demand does this show?

options.text_md: Expectation of a further rise in price
A Giffen good
An emergency
Composite demand

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Expectation of a further rise in price. Buyers expect the price to keep rising, so they buy more as the price rises: the expectations exception.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Every Giffen good is an inferior good, but not every inferior good is a Giffen good.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** A Giffen good must have a negative income effect (inferior); but most inferior goods still obey the law because their substitution effect is stronger, so the statement is true.

questions.stem_md: Why can the demand for a status good, such as a designer handbag, rise when its price rises?
questions.solution_md: Status display and exclusivity linked to price.

answer.model_answer_md: Such a good is bought to **display wealth and status** (a **Veblen** good). A higher price makes it **more exclusive**, so wealthy buyers value it more and buy more of it; a lower price would reduce its appeal.

marking_scheme.step: Higher price raises appeal, so more is bought

questions.stem_md: Very poor families in an imagined drought-hit village spend most of their income on a cheap staple grain. When its price rises, they buy more of it and less of costlier foods. Explain this behaviour.
questions.solution_md: Inferior staple with a large budget share, dominant income effect, conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md: The grain is an **inferior staple** taking a **large share of the budget**. A price rise cuts their **real income** sharply (a strong negative **income effect**), so they can no longer afford costlier foods and fall back on even more of the staple. This income effect **outweighs the substitution effect**, so quantity demanded rises with price: a **Giffen good**.

marking_scheme.step: Inferior good with large budget share

questions.stem_md: Explain any four exceptions to the Law of Demand, with an imagined Indian example of each, and state why each is an exception.
questions.solution_md: Four exceptions, each with an example and the reason it is an exception.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Giffen goods:** very poor households buy more of a cheap inferior staple when its price rises, because the income effect dominates.
2. **Veblen goods:** rich buyers want more of an expensive designer watch at a higher price, for status.
3. **Expectations of price change:** if buyers expect gold to get dearer, they buy more now even as its price rises.
4. **Emergencies:** during a flood families buy more medicines and drinking water despite higher prices.
In each case more is bought at a higher price (or the usual assumptions such as constant expectations no longer hold), so the inverse relation fails.

questions.stem_md:
Read the imagined situation and answer both parts.

A tea stall near a bus stand in an imagined Bhubaneswar locality sells tea at ₹10 a cup. (i) In the first week of winter it sells many more cups at the same price. (ii) A month later the owner cuts the price to ₹8 and sells still more. Identify the change in demand in each part and describe a separate diagram for each. [2 + 2]
questions.solution_md: Classify each change by its cause, then describe the matching diagram.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The price is unchanged but more is bought because **colder weather** raises the desire for tea (a change in tastes or seasonal need): an **increase in demand**. Diagram: at ₹10 the curve shifts **right** from D₁ to D₂, so the quantity rises from Q₁ to Q₂.
(ii) Only the **own price** fell (₹10 to ₹8), so buyers move **down along** the existing curve: an **extension of demand**. Diagram: one curve D, with the point moving from (Q₁, ₹10) to a larger quantity at ₹8.

marking_scheme.step: (i) increase in demand identified with cause

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about an imagined Hyderabad grocery market. [2 + 2]

(i) The price of ragi flour rises, and families buy more jowar flour. What is the relationship between the two goods, and what happens to the demand curve for jowar flour?
(ii) A shopkeeper says that when the price of an expensive imported olive oil rose, a few rich customers bought more of it. Is this consistent with the Law of Demand? Justify.
questions.solution_md: Substitute relation with a rightward shift; Veblen exception with justification.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Ragi and jowar flour are **substitutes**: a dearer ragi flour makes buyers switch to jowar, so the **demand curve for jowar flour shifts to the right** (an increase in demand) at every price of jowar.
(ii) **Not consistent** with the usual law: the oil is bought partly for **status (a Veblen good)**, so its appeal rises with its price. It is an **exception** to the law, which assumes ordinary goods bought for their use.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [4 + 4]

(i) The weekly demands of two imagined households in a Kochi housing society for banana chips are Q = 8 − 0.1P (household A) and Q = 6 − 0.05P (household B), with P in ₹ per packet and no negative quantities. Prepare the market schedule at ₹40, ₹60, ₹80 and ₹100 and explain how the market curve is obtained.
(ii) A festival then raises both households' desire for banana chips. Explain with a described diagram how the market demand curve changes, and contrast this with the effect of a fall in the price of chips.
questions.solution_md: Correct schedule and summation with the kink; then shift versus movement.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i)

| Price (₹) | A | B | Market |
|---|---|---|---|
| 40 | 4 | 4 | 8 |
| 60 | 2 | 3 | 5 |
| 80 | 0 | 2 | 2 |
| 100 | 0 | 1 | 1 |

At each price the two quantities are **added** (horizontal summation). Above ₹80 only B buys, so the market curve follows B's curve; below ₹80 both buy, so the curve is flatter, with a **kink at ₹80**.
(ii) A festival is a change in **tastes** (a non-price determinant): both households want more at every price, so the market curve **shifts right** from D₁ to D₂. A **fall in the price** of chips instead moves buyers **down along the same curve** (an extension); the curve itself does not move.

marking_scheme.step: Festival as a change in tastes
Rightward shift of the market curve
Clear contrast of shift and movement

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [4 + 4]

(i) "A downward-sloping demand curve follows from the way households respond to a price change." Explain this statement using the substitution effect, the income effect and diminishing marginal utility, with examples from an imagined Indian household.
(ii) Evaluate whether the Law of Demand holds in every market by discussing any four situations in which more may be bought at a higher price.
questions.solution_md: Three mechanisms linked to the slope; four exceptions with a judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) When the price of pulses falls: the **substitution effect** makes pulses cheaper relative to vegetables, so the family substitutes towards pulses; the **income effect** raises its real income, so it can buy more pulses; and because **marginal utility diminishes**, it buys extra kilograms only at the lower price. All three make quantity demanded rise as price falls, so the curve **slopes downward**.
(ii) The law does **not** hold everywhere. **Giffen goods:** very poor families buy more of a dearer inferior staple because the income effect dominates. **Veblen goods:** status goods such as luxury cars are wanted more when dearer. **Expectations:** buyers expecting further price rises buy more now. **Emergencies:** during floods or epidemics essentials are bought regardless of price. So the law is a useful **general tendency** under ceteris paribus, not a rule without exceptions.

marking_scheme.step: Evaluation: general tendency under ceteris paribus

questions.stem_md: Read the imagined diary entry of a shopkeeper in an imagined Varanasi lane and answer the questions that follow. *(Written by SOYL for practice.)*
